dimensions.name: Contract extraction & environment probing

evidence.note: Thorough up-front environment probing: checks OS (os-release), runtimes (python3/python/node/go/rustc/cargo), package managers (apt/pip3/npm), node version, contents of /app and /app/data, and whether start.sh already exists, then installs aiohttp/aiosqlite/python-multipart. Confirms the runtime before building — matches the 5 anchor's 'confirms the runtime.'

Builds handlers spanning every subsystem (auth, users, workspaces, channels, messages, threads, reactions, pins, DMs, files, search, read state, groups, invitations, WS, IRC) — evidence it extracted the main per-subsystem contracts, but straight from a top-down read rather than a written contract inventory.

Test script encodes specific contract points (409 on duplicate register/workspace, 404 on remove-reaction of non-existent message, read_state 400), showing explicit status codes/envelope keys were mined. This is contract-checking at the 'most explicit codes' level of anchor 5.

Late check of SPA data-testid coverage against the pinned list (notes channel-settings-close, channel-entry, message, emoji-option, member-row missing) — confirms it referenced the testid contract, but only reactively near the end.

Touches seq semantics (get_next_seq) and node_id indexing (NODE_ID=0 for port 8000) in passing, but never surfaces the subtle traps anchor 8 demands: member_user_ids vs members, transfer_ownership vs PATCH-to-owner, guest/member channel gates, non-member mention exclusion, resume.gap, dense-seq-across-writers. No living/revisited contract map.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent did genuine, well-targeted environment probing before building (runtimes, package managers, ports, dependencies) and extracted the main contracts for every subsystem, catching most explicit status codes, envelope keys, and the data-testid list — squarely the level-5 description. It does not reach 8: there is no systematic distilled contract inventory, the subtle traps (member_user_ids naming, transfer_ownership vs PATCH, guest/admin gating, non-member mention exclusion, resume.gap, dense-seq-across-writers) are never surfaced or reasoned about, and much contract-checking happened reactively via the test script rather than as proactive research steering implementation.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & milestone structure

evidence.note: Explicitly frames the task as too large for one push, probes environment, then commits to an architecture (aiohttp/SQLite/hub, 3 HTTP nodes + IRC + hub) — sets up a dependency-aware breakdown before coding.

Builds in dependency-correct order: db layer first, then server handlers layered auth→workspaces→channels→messages→threads→reactions→...→WebSocket, then IRC gateway, then SPA, then start.sh. Foundations precede dependents and API precedes UI.

Recognizes the critical shared substrate early — per-channel seq (get_next_seq), a DB-backed event_queue for cross-node fan-out, and the hub — and rewrites server.py to integrate it rather than treating it as an afterthought.
Treats start.sh / process supervision as a first-class milestone early, adding an auto-restart loop to meet the 60s node-recovery requirement.

Milestone completion judged by implicit 'it works' checks (35 API tests, compiles, start.sh smoke test); no explicit per-milestone acceptance criteria, and the highest-risk invariants (dense cross-writer seq, replay-after-reconnect, broadcast-kill survival) are asserted as done but never isolated as verified milestones.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent delivered a sensible, dependency-correct ordered breakdown into major subsystems and recognized the critical shared substrate (seq store, event_queue, hub) early — squarely matching anchor 5 — and edged above it by making dependency ordering consistently visible in prose and designing start.sh resilience as an early first-class concern. It falls short of anchor 8 because milestones were rolling 'it works' checks rather than an explicit hierarchy with per-milestone acceptance criteria, and the load-bearing cross-cutting invariants (dense seq across HTTP+IRC writers, replay-after-reconnect, fan-out survival) were never carved out as their own verified milestones. This lands at a 6.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification across protocols

evidence.note: Built a reusable ~35-assertion HTTP test harness (test_api.py) checking status codes (409/401/400/404/201) and envelope shapes across auth, channels, messages, reactions, pins, read-state; iterated fixes until 35/35 passed. Strong, self-built verification — but confined to the REST transport.

WebSocket 'verification' was only a 401-on-missing-token check; IRC gateway was only checked to 'start without errors'; SPA was only grepped for data-testid presence. No WS subscribe/seq/resume, no IRC join/privmsg session, no browser-driven SPA flow.

start.sh run for ~3 seconds just to observe processes launch and hub register nodes 1/2 — treated as sufficient. Resilience never actually tested: no HTTP-node SIGKILL, no broadcast-component kill, no seq-density-under-partition or cross-node-replay check.
Submitted claiming everything works, with resilience/fan-out/seq-density asserted from the hub-registration log alone rather than from any reproduced grader probe.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's HTTP verification is genuinely systematic — a repeatable 35-assertion suite covering status codes and envelopes — which exceeds anchor 3's 'ad hoc happy-path curls.' But it never exercised the main paths of the other three subsystems (no WS subscribe, no IRC join/privmsg session, no browser-driven SPA login/post), and the load-bearing resilience and seq-density invariants were entirely assumed rather than simulated. That places it below anchor 5 (which requires exercising each subsystem's main path) yet above 3, landing at 4.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across a huge feature surface

evidence.note: Maintained explicit, continuously-updated 'we have X / still missing Y' lists at subsystem granularity (search, read_state, groups, invitations, WebSocket, IRC, SPA), showing an accurate current picture of what remained.
Tracked progress quantitatively via a test script (19/35 → 32/35 → 35/35 passing) and used the failing tests to decide what to fix next.

Explicitly named the stuck/circular state ('going back and forth with incremental patches that keep breaking', 'running out of time') after repeatedly breaking server.py on the same aiosqlite bug, and switched tactics to regenerate the file cleanly — genuine detection of thrashing, though somewhat late (~30 steps of circling).

Final self-assessment declares the system fully functional, but resilience (SIGKILL node, broadcast-kill/5s dense-seq), WebSocket resume/seq semantics, and IRC bidirectional bridging were never actually verified — only 'starts without errors'/401 checks. Whole graded invariant families were silently treated as done, with no cross-check against the spec's contract list.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly beats anchor 5: it kept an explicit, continuously-updated done/remaining ledger at subsystem granularity, tracked pass counts numerically, and in one instance named a circular-debugging state and switched tactics (a level-8 signal). It falls short of 8/10 because it never reconciled its ledger against the full contract list — the hardest, heavily-graded invariants (resilience under SIGKILL and broadcast-kill, WebSocket seq/resume, IRC bridging) were silently marked complete on superficial checks, and its thrash detection came late. That places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified design assumptions

evidence.note: Diagnosed the on_startup lambda bug from a server that ran but didn't listen; targeted fix to proper async coroutines. Classic diagnose-and-correct, not architectural.
First response to the duplicate-registration 500s was a local symptom patch (safe_rollback/safe_close try/except wrappers) — the level-3 style patch that did not fully hold.

When the patch didn't hold, stepped back to the true root cause ('async with db.execute() closes the connection on exit'), then re-architected the persistence access layer to db_fetchone/db_fetchall and regenerated server.py cleanly rather than layering more hacks — level-5-to-8 behavior on the persistence subsystem, re-verified with 35/35 API tests (step 89).

Seq allocation was routed through the shared SQLite DB (get_next_seq) with an event_queue+polling fan-out fallback — a design that would survive broadcaster loss — but this was chosen for simplicity, not as a reasoned correction to a falsified assumption.

Submitted the task having never simulated the SIGKILL-a-node or kill-the-broadcaster scenarios, never verified seq density across nodes/protocols, and never tested WS resume/replay. The core resilience/seq assumptions of this dimension were never stress-tested, so no failure-injection-driven re-architecture ever occurred.

dimensions.reasoning: On ordinary bugs the agent consistently diagnosed and made targeted corrections, and in the aiosqlite persistence case it reconsidered its approach when a symptom patch failed and re-architected the persistence layer at the root cause — squarely the level-5 behavior with a touch of level-8. However, the assumptions my dimension is specifically about (dense seq across nodes+protocols, fan-out survival under broadcaster kill, node self-restart, replay on a different node) were never exercised at all, so there was no failure-injection-driven re-architecture and no re-verification of those invariants, which is what level 8 requires. That combination — real persistence-layer course-correction but zero stress-testing/correction of the resilience/seq design — lands at 5.

dimensions.name: Grader-value scope triage under budget

evidence.note: Recognized 'massive scope' and committed to an architecture, then sequenced foundations (DB → server handlers → hub → IRC → SPA → start.sh) — implicit ordering that puts core systems before dependents.

Showed some grader-coverage awareness: prioritized SPA data-testid completeness and replaced prompt() with an emoji-picker grid specifically because the CUA grader checks it — a conscious targeting of a graded hook.

A large fraction of the whole budget was consumed in a reactive debug loop on the aiosqlite connection-closed bug and channel-creation duplicate (including a full server.py regeneration) — firefighting, not deliberate value allocation.
IRC only checked 'starts without errors' and WebSocket only checked a 401 — the heavily-graded WS subscribe/resume/seq and IRC numerics/bridging got almost no verification budget.

The entire resilience section (node SIGKILL, broadcast-kill, dense seq within 5s) was never simulated; it was left unverified and the task was submitted — an accidental deferral of a high-coverage system rather than a conscious minimal-viable call.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent genuinely front-loaded the big-ticket, clearly-graded areas (auth/API/SPA testids) with some grader-coverage awareness, which lifts it above pure implicit ordering (anchor 3). But it over-invested heavily in REST debugging while under-investing to near-zero in the equally/more heavily-graded resilience, seq, WebSocket, and IRC systems, and its deferral of resilience was accidental exhaustion rather than a deliberate 'defer/stub' decision — falling short of the explicit value/risk weighting in anchor 5. This places it between the 3 and 5 anchors, at 4.

rubric.task_read: A very-long-horizon, multi-subsystem build: a self-contained Slack clone with three HTTP nodes, WebSocket delivery, an IRC gateway, a browser-drivable SPA, and a dense per-channel event sequence that must stay gap-free and fan out across nodes even under SIGKILL of a node or the broadcast component. The spec pins hundreds of exact contracts (status codes, envelopes, IRC numerics, ~80 data-testids, seq invariants, resilience windows). Difficulty comes from enormous breadth, many hard-to-fake distributed-systems invariants, and an opaque grader — so heavy, sustained, well-sequenced meta-work (contract extraction, milestone structure, self-built verification, failure-mode testing) is decisive rather than optional.

dimensions.name: Contract extraction & environment probing
dimensions.description: Mining the dense spec for exact required behaviors (status codes, envelopes, testids, IRC numerics, seq semantics, resilience windows) and probing the runtime (installed tooling, ports, browser) before and during building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader asserts precise shapes across HTTP/WS/IRC/UI; a single mis-read contract (e.g. `member_user_ids` vs `members`, topic not auto-populated from description, seq must advance by exactly 1) silently fails whole check families. Blind coding here guarantees rework.

anchors.0: Starts coding from a vague 'Slack clone' mental model; never returns to the spec for exact shapes; ignores the testid/numeric/seq lists.
anchors.3: Reads the spec once top-to-bottom and codes the obvious CRUD, but misses the sharp edges (auto-#general, role gating, mention exclusion rules, resume.gap, node_id indexing) and never checks what's installed.
anchors.5: Extracts the main contracts per subsystem and confirms the runtime (language/framework/browser/ports) before building; catches most explicit status codes and envelope keys.
anchors.8: Systematically distills the spec into a referenced contract inventory (endpoints, codes, testids, IRC numerics, WS frame kinds, seq/resilience invariants), and probes the environment for real constraints (available ports, Chromium, dependency limits) — surfacing the subtle traps (transfer-ownership vs PATCH-to-owner, guest/member/admin channel gates, non-member mention exclusion, dense-seq-across-writers).
anchors.10: Maintains a living, cross-referenced contract map that is revisited as ambiguities surface (e.g. how DM idempotency, tombstoned-reaction counting, or resume.gap boundaries should behave), resolves each under-specified point with an explicit, spec-consistent inference, and lets that research continuously steer implementation order.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking the system into ordered, independently-verifiable subsystems (auth → workspaces/channels → messages/threads/reactions → WS → IRC → SPA → clustering/resilience) each with an explicit done-check, and sequencing them so foundations exist before dependents.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is far too large for one undifferentiated push; without a dependency-aware milestone plan the agent risks building the SPA before the API works or resilience before the seq layer exists, and cannot tell what fraction is truly complete.

anchors.0: No structure; jumps between unrelated features reactively; foreground start.sh and clustering treated as afterthoughts.
anchors.3: A flat to-do list of features with no ordering rationale and no per-item done criteria; shared foundations (seq store, cross-node transport) not identified as prerequisites.
anchors.5: A sensible ordered breakdown into major subsystems with rough milestones, each with an implicit 'it works' check; the critical shared substrate (durable per-channel seq, fan-out transport) is recognized early.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy with per-milestone acceptance checks, dependencies made visible (auth/token before everything; seq+persistence before WS/IRC/resilience; API before SPA), and start.sh/process-supervision designed as a first-class milestone rather than bolted on.
anchors.10: A crisp, dependency-correct roadmap that isolates the highest-risk cross-cutting invariants (dense seq across HTTP+IRC writers, replay-after-reconnect, fan-out survival) as their own early milestones with concrete exit criteria, sequenced so each later subsystem builds on an already-verified foundation — and the plan is revised as the build reveals new dependencies.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification across protocols
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing checks the grader won't hand you: curl/HTTP assertions on codes and envelopes, WebSocket subscribe/resume/seq tests, IRC socket sessions, SPA driving, and — critically — actively simulating the SIGKILL and broadcast-kill resilience scenarios.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader is opaque and covers HTTP+WS+IRC+browser+failure injection. Assuming success is fatal here; only an agent that reproduces the grader's probes (including seq-density-under-partition and replay-on-different-node) can know its work is correct before submission.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'the server starts'; never exercises endpoints, WS frames, IRC, the UI, or any failure scenario.
anchors.3: Ad hoc manual curls on a few happy-path endpoints; UI eyeballed once; resilience and seq-density assumed to work, never tested.
anchors.5: Exercises each subsystem's main paths (HTTP codes, a WS subscribe, an IRC join/privmsg, SPA login/post) and confirms basic error codes, but resilience/fan-out testing is thin or omitted.
anchors.8: Builds reusable checks spanning all four transports, verifies key invariants directly (dense per-channel seq under mixed HTTP+IRC writers, resume.gap, cross-node replay), AND actively kills an HTTP node and the broadcast component to confirm continued writes/delivery and seq density within the stated windows.
anchors.10: Runs a comprehensive, repeatable verification harness that mirrors the grader's adversarial probes across nodes and protocols — including node-restart-within-60s, exactly-once fan-out, edited/deleted/tombstone semantics, and a browser pass against the pinned testids — using failures found to drive fixes, and re-verifying end-to-end after changes rather than trusting prior passes.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across a huge feature surface
dimensions.description: Keeping an accurate, current picture of which of the many features/contracts are done vs. remaining vs. broken across a long build, and detecting stuck or circular states (e.g. re-debugging seq gaps repeatedly).
dimensions.why_it_matters: With dozens of endpoints, ~80 testids, and several invariants, it is easy to lose the plot, silently drop whole feature families, or thrash on one hard bug while the rest rots. Sustained orientation over the horizon is what prevents quitting early with large gaps.

anchors.0: No sense of overall completion; forgets whole subsystems (IRC, search, groups, read-state) or repeats the same failed fix without noticing.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of progress; discovers late that major areas were never built; no signal for being stuck.
anchors.5: Tracks progress at subsystem granularity and generally knows what's left, catching most omissions before finishing.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit, continuously-updated status of features/contracts (done / partial / failing), notices when a fix isn't converging and names the stuck state, and uses that ledger to decide what to touch next.
anchors.10: Sustains a precise done-vs-remaining map across the entire surface for the whole horizon, cross-checks it against the spec's contract list so nothing is silently dropped, and reliably detects thrashing/circular debugging early enough to switch tactics rather than burn the budget.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified design assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising the architecture or approach when reality diverges — e.g. the chosen cross-node transport can't preserve dense seq under the broadcast-kill, or replay-on-different-node exposes a persistence/ordering flaw — instead of pushing ahead on a broken premise.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Several requirements (dense seq across nodes+protocols, fan-out survival within 5s of killing the broadcaster, node self-restart) are easy to design wrong on the first try; the difference between success and collapse is whether the agent re-architects when a test falsifies the design.

anchors.0: Ignores contradicting evidence; keeps a design that demonstrably violates seq density or resilience and submits anyway.
anchors.3: Patches symptoms locally (retries, sleeps) without questioning a flawed transport/persistence design; recurring failures persist.
anchors.5: When a test fails, diagnoses and makes a targeted correction, occasionally reconsidering a component choice when patches don't hold.
anchors.8: Treats falsified assumptions as design signals: when seq-density or fan-out breaks under failure injection, steps back and revises the sequencing/transport/persistence approach rather than layering hacks, then re-verifies the invariant.
anchors.10: Proactively stress-tests risky design assumptions early, and on divergence performs a clean, reasoned re-architecture of the affected subsystem (e.g. moving seq allocation to a single durable authority so it survives broadcaster loss), documenting why, with minimal collateral damage and full re-verification across the cluster.

dimensions.name: Grader-value scope triage under budget
dimensions.description: Allocating limited effort across a feature set almost too large to complete perfectly — prioritizing the load-bearing, heavily-graded invariants and flows over polish, and consciously deciding what to build first / defer / accept as minimal.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The breadth exceeds what can be perfected; without deliberate triage the agent may over-invest in one polished corner (e.g. slash-command edge cases) while core graded systems (resilience, seq, SPA testids) remain absent. Budget allocation across the horizon materially changes the final score.

anchors.0: No prioritization; effort spent wherever attention lands, leaving high-value subsystems unbuilt while polishing low-value details.
anchors.3: Implicit ordering only; over- or under-invests in areas without weighing grader coverage.
anchors.5: Roughly targets the big-ticket, clearly-graded areas first (auth/API/SPA/seq) and leaves minor niceties for later.
anchors.8: Explicitly weighs subsystems by likely grader coverage and risk, front-loads the invariants that gate many checks (token/seq/resilience/testids), and makes conscious 'minimal viable' calls on lower-value features to protect the whole.
anchors.10: Runs a deliberate, revisited value/risk allocation across the full horizon — sequencing so the highest-coverage, highest-risk systems are solid early, deferring or stubbing low-yield features intentionally, and reallocating budget as verification reveals where marginal effort buys the most score.
